chapter_theme: Akananuru 361 to 380, from the நித்திலக்கோவை section: nine paalai poems of men arguing with their hearts on the road to wealth and of wives and mothers left behind, set among kurinji night and day trysts pressing for marriage, two mullai rain poems, two marutham sulks and two neythal meetings, with Pazhi, Kaamur, Evvi, Uranthai and the Atthi legend used as scales of comparison.

361.reading: On the wide hot track he has already entered, the man tells his heart, which would not take his word that nothing surpasses the embrace of a girl who sulks if even a thread comes between them, and chose wealth instead, to stop thinking of her shoulders now, as a turtle dropped in a pot over the fire longs in vain for the shaded pool.
361.nuance: The argument the heart rejected is quoted in full, so the poem's real speaker is the losing side of a debate: the man has already obeyed the heart and gone, and his order to it to stop remembering is the measure of how much he remembers. The turtle in the pot pictures a longing that comes too late; the phrase about the elders in line 10 (கரியாப் பூவின் பெரியோர்) is obscure, but the turtle's plight is clear without it.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left his wife for wealth and is crossing the wasteland

comparisons.vehicle: தாமரைப் பூவின் அங்கண் மாஇதழ்க் குவளை மலர்பிணைத்
comparisons.tenor: her eyes set in her face
the heart longing for the girl it has left

362.reading: With the hero hidden nearby, the friend tells the girl that the hill streams are in flood and the path is shut by a tigress guarding her mate, wounded by an elephant, so that if the good man who came by night with his spear goes back with nothing, she will not live a day; and she asks why the moon has made the night as bright as the necklace on their breasts and the white waterfall.
362.nuance: Every danger she lists is the man's, and the bright moon is a further danger to secret meeting, so the speech to the girl is a warning to the listener that night visits cannot go on; it presses toward marriage without naming it. The tigress keeping watch over her wounded mate stays a sign of the path's danger here: the poem draws nothing from her care.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிச் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: hill streams, tiger in the rock cave and the waterfall of the slope, with a night tryst

363.reading: As the sun's chariot sets behind the mountain, the friend tells the girl, faded like a flower past its hour and lying on her bed, not to grieve: the man who crossed the cruel wasteland, where the wind scatters gooseberries like gold coins on the stony path and the hawk calls its kin to men speared by waiting robbers, has done his work and is coming back, so that her eyes will regain their beauty.
363.nuance: The terrors of the road are given at length only to be put behind: they are the measure of what he has already passed, and so of how sure his return now is. The gooseberries that look like gold coins hint at the wealth he went for, lying on the very road of danger.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot wasteland and its robbers, crossed by the absent man

364.reading: The girl tells her friend that the rains have come with thunder, frogs drum in every hollow, the kondrai hangs like gold, thondri and mullai bloom and the rock pools fill, yet her lover, in the great camp of a king eager for victory, does not think of them; and the evening that comes like one bent on killing is too much to swim through.
364.nuance: The season he promised to return by is described as complete and lovely, and only then measured against his absence; the more perfect the rains, the plainer it is that he has broken his word. The camp belongs to a king, not to him: he stays for another man's victory.

colophon.thurai: பருவங் கண்டழிந்த தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the onset of the rains and the waiting wife, with the flowers of the woodland

365.reading: At dusk in the burning wasteland, where wild elephants kick a hero-stone taking it for a man and snap their nails, and fallen bowmen lie with none to tend them, the man tells his heart, which brought him there and, unable to bear the pain it caused, now thinks of turning back, that it is the girl's soft dark hair, fragrant with the new vengai flowers of Kazhuvul's Kaamur, that draws it.
365.nuance: The heart that drove him out is the same heart that now wants to go home; the poem catches it in the act of changing sides. Kaamur's vengai, given by a spirit, makes her hair a thing of a famous and blessed place set against the desolate place he stands in. Lines 7 and 8 are hard to construe, and the turn in lines 10 and 11 can be read as rebuke or as relief.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்து நின்று சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer wasteland with its hero-stones, where the parted man stands

366.reading: Refusing the husband entry, the friend tells him that their lady, lovely as a goddess, wept when she learned he had wronged her yesterday by staying in a fragrant grove with the bright-browed girl whose shoulders are as comforting as the shade of Evvi, the lord who, when farmers and salt-makers came to blows over salt pans spoilt by threshing chaff, had the grey elders part them and gave toddy to the fishermen.
366.nuance: The long scene of the brawl belongs to the simile: it shows Evvi as a peacemaker and giver, and so makes the rival's shoulders a place of shelter and peace, a generous praise of the other woman that sharpens the wife's tears. The friend's charge is in two words, நீதற் பிழைத்தமை: you wronged her.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையிற் பிரிந்துவந்த தலைமகன் வாயில் வேண்டியவிடத்துத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's straying and the wife's weeping, the sulk of the field country

367.reading: Answering the friend who urges her to bear up, the girl says that the dreary evening, when the old bull bellows, the cattle rest by the nochchi hedge of the frontier hamlet and the male civet lies in wait by the millet store to seize the red-combed rooster and ease his hungry mate, must indeed be sweet to those who hold close their faultless companion, whose softness makes life melt at every embrace.
367.nuance: She never says the evening is bitter for her; she says it is sweet for the joined, and lets the friend draw the rest. Inside that sweet scene the civet hunting for his mate is the one creature that provides for a partner at nightfall.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் வற்புறுக்கும் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the parted wife's evening, measured against the joined

iraicchi.act: the male civet lies in wait to catch the rooster and ease the tired hunger of his mate
iraicchi.sense: even a wild male stays at nightfall to feed his mate, while her own man has gone and left her to the evening alone

368.reading: With the hero hidden by day, the friend asks the girl why, when the hill lord, in whose land the vengai flowers like a peahen's crest above the millet-guarding girls' swing, played with them like a tusker with his cow in a clear spring of a grove no monkey reaches, and went away for many days, gossip has grown in the toddy-drinking hamlet, in many mouths, like the Ulli festival of the Kongar who dance in the streets with bells at their waists.
368.nuance: The question is for the listener: the meeting was rare and long ago, yet the talk is already as loud as a festival, so secret love can no longer stay secret. The day tryst is at a place no monkey can reach, which makes the town's knowing all the stranger.

colophon.thurai: பகலே சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகட்குத் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill farmer's millet plot and vengai, with a day tryst

comparisons.tenor: the clear water of the spring

369.reading: The foster mother grieves that, since the girl went, the parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play, the potted plant gets no flowers and the doll no offering; she missed the girl's purpose when she offered to wash her hair, and the girl, hurt, refused the rich wedding her kin were preparing in a house like Uranthai of the Cholas, and went over the wasteland with a young man of steady heart and long spear, and now the mother wonders whether her daughter had her anklets taken off in a poor woman's grass hut with one pillar and one cow, without honour or ceremony.
369.nuance: The house is described through the girl's things left without her, and the grief turns at the end from her loss to her status: what hurts is that the anklet-removal of a wedding happened in a stranger's poor hut. The words கண்டிசின் மகளே (line 1) address someone the speaker calls daughter; whether it is the girl's own mother is not clear from the poem.

colophon.thurai: மகட் போக்கிய செவிலி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has left home with her lover across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: the girls of the play group
the rich house of the planned wedding

370.reading: With the hero hidden by day, the friend reminds the girl that she once said that if, after playing with them in the punnai shade by day, he lay lovesick at night, she would fall under her father's strict guard, and that she cannot bring herself to tell him not to go yet says she will not live if he goes; so, with the girl staying in the grove like the sea goddess on the shore at dusk, the friend cannot bear to go home stripped of her own finery like a dancing girl, and says let the town talk.
370.nuance: Whose words are quoted in lines 1 to 9, and who will 'fall under guard', can be read more than one way; on any reading the friend's closing அலர்கவிவ் வூரே is spoken for the man to hear, daring the gossip so that he will end it by marriage.

colophon.thurai: பகலே சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai shade, shore flowers and the grove by the sea

comparisons.tenor: the girl lingering in the grove

371.reading: Crossing alone the scorched waste where a twist-horned stag, his mate shot by hunters, grieves with the fawns playing at his side, refuses to graze, will not drink the little water of the pond and lies down stricken like a speared man, the man asks his heart what will become of his beloved's eyes, which bees take for flowers of a clear spring, streaming tears even more than he.
371.nuance: He measures her grief by his own and finds hers greater: the stag, who has really lost his mate, is the image of what the man's going does to the one left. The fawns playing unaware at the stag's side make the loss sharper.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the scorched waste the parted man crosses alone

iraicchi.act: the stag whose mate was shot refuses food and water and lies grieving for her
iraicchi.sense: even a beast pines when parted from its mate, so his leaving will waste the woman he leaves behind

372.reading: Turning back from a tryst that a false signal spoiled, the man tells his heart, which would not accept that the girl is as hard to win as the treasure the old Velir hid in their city at Pazhi under a dread god's guard, that it has swung to and fro like a swing-rope on a tall palm, tightened and slackened like the strap of a raider's war drum, and pined like a snake that has lost its gem, for she is guarded closer than a kings' fortress.
372.nuance: Each simile measures the hardness of the girl's guard, and each is one the hero may use openly. The poem shares its opening thought and its turn எனினும் அஃது ஒல்லாய் with Akananuru 258, which is under the same occasion.

colophon.thurai: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்டுப் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the secret lover's failed night meeting with a closely guarded girl

comparisons.tenor: the girl's being hard to win

373.reading: Worn out by the wasteland and sitting alone at a desolate dusk with his hands round his knees, in the ruined hall of a village emptied by raiders where an elephant rubs against the rotting post, the man pictures the girl, who knows her own state but not his, lying on her bed at midnight sighing and sulking, flicking away with her nails the tears that soak her shoulders, and asks whether she has given up sleep like the king of a single fort besieged by many kings, poor girl.
373.nuance: He imagines her blaming him (புலக்கும் நெஞ்சமொடு) because she cannot see that he too is suffering: the pity of the last line is partly for himself. The besieged chieftain is an image of sleepless watching against odds.

colophon.thurai: பிரிந்து போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the raided, deserted village on the wasteland road

374.reading: His campaign over, the man tells his charioteer to drive on in this lovely morning of the rains, when clouds that drank the sea flash and pour sweetly without thunder, like a bard's tuned lute, and on the sandy track the red mites run, like coral among sapphires, hiding among the fallen kaayaa blossoms, so that the slender girl may welcome him as a guest.
374.nuance: The rain is made gentle and musical, without thunder, because for him it is now a season of return, not of reproach. The last word, விருந்து, makes the husband a guest to be received, the honour of a homecoming.

colophon.thurai: பாசறை முற்றிய தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains' morning on the woodland track, with kaayaa and red mites

comparisons.tenor: the soft sound of the rain
the red mites among the kaayaa blossoms

375.reading: To the friend who said he will not stay away long, the girl answers that if she knew that the man who crossed the dread wasteland, where raw youths kill even empty-handed travellers to test their arrows and feed the birds, and where the vulture, its claws wet with blood, perched on the white yaa trunk looks like the tusk of an elephant of Ilamperunchenni, the Chola who broke Pazhi's copper-strong walls and crushed the Vadukar, would come back unharmed, her eyes would not weep.
375.nuance: Her answer turns the friend's comfort from 'he will return soon' to 'will he return alive': her fear is not delay but death on the road. The Chola's war elephant, the vulture and the arrows make the wasteland a battlefield.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wasteland of killers and vultures crossed by the absent man

comparisons.tenor: the vulture on the white trunk

376.reading: The beloved courtesan tells the lord not to go: once she owed him every duty, but now, as the Kaveri seized and hid Atthi when he danced adorned in its flood at Kazhar before Karikal and his crowd, he has been taken from her; she will not sulk at him, but let him see her paled brow, give back her beauty, which was like Kuttuvan's Maranthai, and then go.
376.nuance: The Atthi legend is here turned around: the woman who loses the man to the river is not his wife but the courtesan, and the river that keeps him is, by implication, his household. The closing demand நலம்தந்து சென்மே is the same as Akananuru 396's, also a courtesan's. The first two lines are compressed and their sense uncertain.

colophon.thurai: காதற் பரத்தை புலந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the paddy fields and river town, with a courtesan's sulk

comparisons.tenor: the man kept from the courtesan

377.reading: The man tells his heart, which has urged him to go for wealth, that those who can give with renown what people who come in hope ask of them must surely pass their nights as wanderers in some corner of a haunted common hall, its dice board crumbled and its pillars eaten by termites, in a village whose families fled when bowmen raided its cattle and where ants store fallen grass seed, thinking all the while of the soft beauty of their smiling women.
377.nuance: The poem gives the price of the giver's fame: the wealth for giving is earned on roads of ruin, and the giver sleeps among ruins with his wife only in his thoughts. The ants' hoard in the drought-dried field is the one store the raiders could not take.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் கடைக்கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the long drought and the raided, deserted village of the wealth-seeker's road

378.reading: With the hero hidden by night, the girl answers the friend who asked how she can live through the lord's parting, her angry mother's look and the anguished evenings of the cold season, in a land where wind shakes gold-like vengai pollen into brides' hair and the peacock cries sweet as a festival trumpet among the swaying bamboo: though the man who left after an oath does not think of her, she lives because the sky-touching peak of his hill, crowned with a singing waterfall where monkeys snatch jackfruit and frolic with their mates, is in sight.
378.nuance: The friend's question is put so that the hidden man hears the full list of what the girl bears, and the girl's answer, that she lives on the sight of his hill, is a reproach he cannot miss. The pair of monkeys at play in his own land is the togetherness he has denied her.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிச் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி சொல்லெடுப்பத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord's land of vengai, wild goats, monkeys and falls

iraicchi.act: the female monkey, holding the jackfruit she snatched, frolics together with her mate
iraicchi.sense: in his own land even the monkeys keep their mates by them, while he who swore not to leave lives apart from her

379.reading: The man, home once with wealth and now pressed again by his heart, tells it that even sole rule of the sea-girt earth passes like a dream of the night, that he has not yet had his fill of her clinging embrace as she sleeps on his shoulder with her flower-crowned hair, and that if it makes him break his word and go, it will rest in the dappled shade of a burnt leafless forest, be struck by her many virtues, and pine on the endless road where a cow elephant trumpets for her tusker wounded by a tiger.
379.nuance: The argument against going is the impermanence of wealth, a puram commonplace, put to an akam use: since wealth passes, the embrace, not the treasure, is what should be held. The cow elephant crying for her wounded mate is what he expects to hear when the memory of the wife strikes him on the road.

colophon.thurai: முன்னொரு காலத்துப் பெருண்முற்றி வந்த தலைமகன் பின்னும் பொருள் கடைக்கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the heart urging a second journey for wealth across the burnt forest

iraicchi.act: the cow elephant trumpets in distress for her mate wounded by a tiger
iraicchi.sense: a mate cries out for the partner in danger, as the wife left behind will grieve for him on that road

380.reading: The friend, having agreed to help the hero, tells the girl that the lord of the shore who came alone, leaving his chariot far off, and drew near asking the name of their town, went away yesterday thoughtful after showing them a crab that tore a naaval fruit at the ford and carried it to its mate in its burrow under the screwpine, saying 'this is a fine way'; now his chariot is in sight, and he is so modest that if they do not receive him today he may resolve on that; should she hide behind the long white dune?
380.nuance: The man's comment on the crab is his only open speech, and it carries his intent: the crab that brings food home to its mate is the life he offers her. What he 'may resolve on' (அது) is left unsaid, and the friend's last question hands the decision to the girl.

colophon.thurai: பின்னின்ற தலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord, screwpine, crab and dunes

iraicchi.act: the crab breaks off the fruit and carries it to its mate in their burrow
iraicchi.sense: the man who points it out means to take the girl home and provide for her as the crab does for its mate

links.note: Both make the man say that the sweetest thing is an embrace that lets nothing come between: in the Kural not even a breeze, in the poem not even a thread, at which she sulks.
links.teaches: The couplet states the delight as settled, while the poem quotes it as the argument the man lost to his heart's desire for wealth, so the Kural's claim is shown being tested and overruled inside the paalai situation.

links.note: Both are the hero's words to his heart under the same occasion (அல்ல குறி), both liken the girl to the treasure the old Velir guarded at Pazhi, and both turn on எனினும் அஃது ஒல்லாய்.
links.teaches: The repeated opening under one thurai shows a fixed formula for the spoiled night meeting, the Velir's hidden gold at Pazhi standing for the guarded girl, which 258 then ends in the heart's ruin and 372 in a run of similes for its swinging.

links.note: Pazhi is the Velir's god-guarded treasure city in 372 and the copper-walled fort Ilamperunchenni broke in 375.
links.teaches: One fort served akam poets for both halves of its story, as the byword for what cannot be reached and as the scene of a famous breach, so a puram place-name carried opposite meanings depending on which part of its history the speaker needed.

links.note: Kazhuvul's Kaamur is a place of blessed vengai fragrance in 365 and the town thrown into turmoil by the fourteen Velir in 135.
links.teaches: The same chieftain's town gives one poet the image of calm sweetness for the wife's hair and another the image of a besieged, shaken heart, showing that a puram name entered akam with its whole history, peace and siege alike, available for comparison.

links.note: Evvi is the unsparing giver (ஓம்பா ஈகை மாவேள் எவ்வி) in the Purananuru poem and the lord who gives toddy to the fishermen to end a brawl in 366.
links.teaches: The Purananuru names Evvi's giving as a title, while the akam simile shows it as a scene of keeping peace between farmers and salt-makers and makes his shade a measure of a woman's comfort, so a patron's fame for protection became an akam image of shelter.

links.note: Both use the figure of the ஓர்எயில் மன்னன, the chieftain of a single fort set against crowned kings: in 338 he will not give his daughter to them, in 373 he lies sleepless under their siege.
links.teaches: The kaanchi poem on a daughter refused to kings shows where the akam poet's image came from: the lone fort's siege was a known situation of puram, and the akam poet borrowed only its sleepless watch to picture the wife.

links.note: Both are a courtesan's words to the man, both liken his loss to the Kaveri seizing and hiding Atthi, and both end on the demand to give back her beauty and go (நலம்தந்து சென்மே).
links.teaches: Two poems sharing speaker, legend and closing line show that the Atthi story and the 'return my beauty' demand formed a stock courtesan's reproach, which each poet then fitted to a different king's town as the measure of her lost beauty.

links.note: Karikal is the victor of Venni in the Purananuru poem and the onlooker at Atthi's flood-dance at Kazhar in 376.
links.teaches: The conqueror praised in puram appears in akam only as a royal spectator who dates and places a love legend, so akam poets used a war king's fame as a frame for a story of loss rather than of victory.

links.note: The Kural says to give and live with renown (இசைபட) as the only gain; the poem names those who give with renown (இசைபடப் பெய்தல்) as the men who must sleep in ruined halls on the road to wealth.
links.teaches: The poem shows what the Kural's rule costs a married man: renown from giving needs wealth, and wealth needs the wasteland and separation, so the maxim's single profit is bought with the akam hero's loneliness.

links.note: Both say great wealth does not last: the Kural likens its coming and going to a crowd at a dance hall, the poem likens its passing to a night's dream.
links.teaches: The poem turns the Kural's general warning about wealth into a reason for a husband to stay home, using impermanence not to urge giving but to set the wife's embrace above a second journey for gain.

links.note: Both are a mother's words after the daughter's elopement; in 15 the mother prays that the town the girl reaches be rich and welcoming to strangers, in 369 the foster mother fears she has married in a poor one-cow hut.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the two laments show that imagining the daughter's new home was a set part of the eloped-daughter situation, and that the poets could make it either a blessing or a wound to family pride.

new_concepts.gloss: the appointed meeting place and time of secret lovers, by day or by night, and the signal that calls the lover to it
marriage as the end of secret love, which the friend presses the lover toward

akananuru:368: the colophon thurai has தலைமகட்குத் சொல்லுவாளாய், a த் before ச that is not regular sandhi, for தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய் (as in 370's colophon); copied as is in `colophon`.
akananuru:369: the flag reports 26 lines in our base text against 27 in the commentary edition (pmuni0534); the lineation differs.
akananuru:373: the flag reports 19 lines in our base text against 18 in the commentary edition (pmuni0534); the lineation differs.
akananuru:379: the colophon thurai has பெருண்முற்றி, probably for பொருண்முற்றி (having completed the wealth); copied as is in `colophon`.
